y-m-32-01.title: If an equation works for several values, does it always work?
y-m-32-01.topic: Meaning of an identity: how many values can settle it?
y-m-32-01.goal: Tell apart how evidence from substituting values supports 'true only for a few values' versus 'true for every x', and adjust how sure you are each time new information comes in.
y-m-32-01.material: Seoa looked at the equation x³ = x and said, "If I plug in numbers like 0, 1, and −1 for x, it will keep working, so it's an equation that holds no matter what number x is." (x³ means 'x cubed'. Here x is a real number.) Check whether Seoa is right by substituting values one at a time.
y-m-32-01.thinking.0: Adjusting your confidence step by step as evidence builds up
y-m-32-01.thinking.1: Exploring the asymmetry between showing something holds and breaking it
y-m-32-01.thinking.2: Judging the power of a single counterexample
y-m-32-01.prereq.0: Calculating the value of a polynomial by substituting numbers for the variable
y-m-32-01.prereq.1: The meaning of an identity as 'an equation that holds for any number x' (introductory level of the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-01.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-01.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think about Seoa's claim.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, count the values tested so far and think about how many untested values are left.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.hint.1: Before new information arrives, say first whether your confidence compared with your earlier judgment has grown or shrunk.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.info: Substituting x=0 gives 0³=0 on the left side and 0 on the right side, so they are equal. Substituting x=1 gives 1³=1 on the left side and 1 on the right side, so they are equal.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think of Seoa's claim based on only these two values?
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.after: The two values x=0 and x=1 do not contradict Seoa's claim, but they do not guarantee 'every x'. It is appropriate to keep the possibility open and test other values.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It worked for two values, so we can conclude it holds for all x without testing other values
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Having some values that work is different from 'every x'. It could fail for values not tested.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is possible, but two values alone cannot settle it, so we test other values too
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment looks at both the number of values tested and the distance to 'every x'.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The two sides being equal at 0 and 1 is just a coincidence, so this test gives no information at all
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The fact that it holds is itself information. It is just not enough to settle the question.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If it worked for two values, it is natural that the same result comes out for untested values too
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This decides in advance the result for untested values. You need evidence.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.info: I also substituted x=−1. The left side is (−1)³=−1 and the right side is −1, so they are equal. Now it holds for all three values 0, 1, and −1.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does your judgment change now?
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Both judgments are reasonable. As more values work, confidence grows a little, but it still does not show 'every x'. It is also a good attitude to suspect that only special values were chosen.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 0, 1, and −1 are easy values and may be a coincidence, so test 2 or 3 too
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment also looks at what kind of values were tested.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It worked for three values in a row, so now it is certain that it holds for all x
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Working three times does not guarantee that it works for the remaining values.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Because it worked three times, it has become more likely that it is not an identity
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: More values worked, and there is no reason yet for going in the opposite direction.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It has become more likely, but it is not settled yet
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Confidence went up as much as the evidence built up, but it was kept separate from being settled.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Substituting x=2 gives 2³=8 on the left side and 2 on the right side, so they are not equal.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you say about Seoa's claim?
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.after: At x=2, 8≠2, so x³=x is not an identity. To show it holds you would have to cover every x, but one value is enough to break it.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It worked for three values and failed for only one, so we can say it is almost an identity
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 'Holds for every x' is not something you judge by the proportion of times it worked.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Treat x=2 as an exception and call it an identity just because it works for 0, 1, and −1
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you remove the exception, the claim 'every x' itself changes.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It might be a calculation mistake, so don't use this value and put off the judgment
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You can check 8 and 2 by calculating directly. Once confirmed, the judgment is settled.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: At x=2 the two sides are different, so it is not an identity. This one value is enough
y-m-32-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: To break 'every', one value where it fails is enough.
y-m-32-01.s.s1.reflect: How did your confidence change at the first two values, the third value, and x=2? In one sentence, say for which conclusions 'testing by plugging in values' is enough and for which it is not enough.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.prompt: What best explains why x³=x holds for x=0, 1, −1 but not for x=2?
y-m-32-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the difference of the two sides, x³−x, as one expression, then find the x values that make it 0.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.hint.1: Plug in one more value such as x=2.5 or x=−2 and check whether the difference is 0.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.o.a: x³−x=x(x−1)(x+1), so the two sides are equal only for values that make one factor 0
y-m-32-01.s.s2.r.a: You rewrote the difference x³−x as a product and found the values where the sides are equal.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.o.b: x³ is always greater than x, so the values where they can be equal are fixed separately
y-m-32-01.s.s2.r.b: Directly compare the sizes of x³ and x when x is between 0 and 1 or when x is negative. It is not always greater.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.o.c: 2 is an integer, so it is a value where the calculation goes wrong, while 0, 1, and −1 are not such values
y-m-32-01.s.s2.r.c: 2 is an integer too. It does not hold because of being an integer.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.o.d: An equation that is not an identity always holds for exactly three values
y-m-32-01.s.s2.r.d: The number of values that work differs from equation to equation. For example, x²=x holds for two values.
y-m-32-01.s.s2.explain: x³−x=x(x−1)(x+1), so it is 0 only when x=0, 1, −1. For any other value, the left and right sides differ, so at x=2 as well, 8≠2.

y-m-32-02.title: Making a cubic expression that satisfies two conditions by yourself
y-m-32-02.topic: Making a polynomial using remainders and factors (undetermined coefficients)
y-m-32-02.goal: Make several cubic expressions that satisfy the given conditions on your own, and tell apart what is determined and what is free given the number of conditions and the number of unknowns.
y-m-32-02.material: You want to make a cubic expression f(x)=x³+ax²+bx+c. a, b, and c are integers. (ax² means 'a times x squared'.) There are two conditions. ① f(x) is divisible by x−1. ② The remainder when f(x) is divided by x+1 is 4. Also, a and c are not 0 (make an expression that has both a quadratic term and a constant term).
y-m-32-02.thinking.0: Turning conditions into equations and making several examples that satisfy them
y-m-32-02.thinking.1: Understanding that when conditions are lacking, the solution is not determined as one
y-m-32-02.thinking.2: Telling apart values that are determined from values that are free
y-m-32-02.prereq.0: The fact that the remainder when a polynomial is divided by x−k equals the value at x=k (introductory level of the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-02.prereq.1: Solving two linear equations with letters as a system (middle school level)
y-m-32-02.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-02.s.s1.prompt: There are 2 conditions but 3 things to determine: a, b, and c. About how many f(x) that satisfy the conditions can you make?
y-m-32-02.s.s1.hint.0: For conditions ① and ②, decide what value to plug in for x in each.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.hint.1: Plug those values into f(x) to make two equations in a, b, and c, and compare the number of equations with the number of unknowns.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.o.a: There are only 2 conditions, so some numbers are left undetermined and we cannot make such a cubic expression
y-m-32-02.s.s1.r.a: Having few conditions does not make it impossible. It is impossible when the conditions contradict each other.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.o.b: If there are conditions, f is always determined as exactly one, and you just find that one by calculation
y-m-32-02.s.s1.r.b: There are 3 unknowns and 2 conditions, so you need to check whether everything is determined.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.o.c: If the conditions do not contradict each other, there are leftover numbers, so you can make several
y-m-32-02.s.s1.r.c: This judgment compares the number of conditions and unknowns to see whether there is leftover freedom.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.o.d: Regardless of the conditions, any integers you choose for a, b, and c all satisfy the conditions
y-m-32-02.s.s1.r.d: You must satisfy conditions ① and ②. Plug in values to check.
y-m-32-02.s.s1.explain: If the conditions do not contradict each other, 2 equations cannot determine all 3 unknowns, so something is left over. We will find out how many are actually determined by making examples ourselves.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different (a, b, c) that satisfy conditions ① and ② and also 'a and c are not 0'.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write what numbers the values obtained by plugging in 1 and −1 for x must be.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one value of a, then adjust b and c so that both conditions are satisfied.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.hint.2: Plug the (a, b, c) you made back into f(1) and f(−1) to check.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, and c are integers.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, and c must be integers.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.fail.c2: f(1) is not 0. Plug 1 in for x and calculate.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The remainder when divided by x+1 is 4 (f(−1)=4).
y-m-32-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The remainder when divided by x+1 is not 4. Plug −1 in for x and calculate.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.fail.c4: a and c must not be 0.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.explain: From f(1)=1+a+b+c=0 and f(−1)=−1+a−b+c=4, we get b=−3 and a+c=2. So b is fixed at −3, and once you choose a, c=2−a follows. Examples: (1, −3, 1), (3, −3, −1), (−2, −3, 4). a=2, c=0 is excluded because c is 0, which breaks the condition.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare the examples you found. a and c could take many values, but b had only one value. Explain in your own words why.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the two conditions as equations in a, b, and c, then add the two equations and subtract them.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare which letter is left when you add and when you subtract.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Writing the two conditions as equations gives ...
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that you wrote the two conditions as equations in a, b, and c?
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you separate the reason b is determined from the reason a and c are free?
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check that all your examples satisfy a+c=2?
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Writing the two conditions as equations gives a+b+c=−1 and a−b+c=5. Subtracting the two equations fixes b as −3, and adding them leaves only one equation, a+c=2. So once a is chosen c follows, and a and c can take many values.
y-m-32-02.s.s2.because.model.1: b=−3 is fixed because subtracting the two equations leaves only b. The only remaining condition is 'the sum of a and c is 2', so any pair of integers whose sum is 2 (1 and 1, 3 and −1, ...) works.

y-m-32-03.title: If an expression is never 0, can it not be split up?
y-m-32-03.topic: Factoring: judging when there is no linear factor
y-m-32-03.goal: Sort out what the evidence 'there is no real value that makes it 0' shows and what it does not show, and revise your judgment when new information (another form of the expression) arrives.
y-m-32-03.material: Minho looked at x⁴+4 and said, "No matter what real number I plug in for x, x⁴+4 is never 0. So this expression cannot be factored any further." (x⁴ means 'x to the fourth power'. Here factoring means writing it as a product of polynomials with integer coefficients.) Examine Minho's conclusion.
y-m-32-03.thinking.0: Telling apart the range that the evidence supports
y-m-32-03.thinking.1: Revising your judgment according to new information
y-m-32-03.prereq.0: The difference of squares formula A²−B²=(A+B)(A−B) (middle school level)
y-m-32-03.prereq.1: Calculating by multiplying polynomials and expanding
y-m-32-03.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-03.s.s1.prompt: New information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think about Minho's conclusion.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether there is a missing step between Minho's observation (it is never 0 for any real number) and his conclusion (it cannot be factored).
y-m-32-03.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the new information changes the observation or changes the basis for the conclusion.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.info: Plugging in 0, 1, −1, and 2 for x gives x⁴+4 values of 4, 5, 5, and 20. For any real number x, x⁴ is 0 or more, so x⁴+4 is 4 or more.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think of Minho's conclusion based on this information?
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.after: No real number makes the value 0, which means there is no factor of the form x−k. Whether it could be a product of two quadratic expressions has to be checked separately, so it is appropriate to see the conclusion as premature.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: We confirmed there is no real root, so we can settle that factoring is impossible
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Having no linear factor is different from being unable to write it as any product.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The fact that it is always 4 or more is information that has nothing to do with whether it can be factored
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: If there were a linear factor x−k, the value would have to be 0 at x=k, so it is related.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: An expression with large values can be expected to split nicely into a product
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is no basis for linking the size of the value to whether it can be factored.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It shows there is no linear factor, but the possibility of a product of two quadratic expressions remains
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You separated the range the observation shows (no linear factor) from the range of the conclusion (cannot be factored).
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.info: You can rewrite x⁴+4 as (x²+2)²−(2x)². (x²+2)²=x⁴+4x²+4 and (2x)²=4x², so the difference is x⁴+4.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think when you see this new form?
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.after: Both judgments are reasonable. In A²−B²=(A+B)(A−B), with A=x²+2 and B=2x, it could become a product of two quadratic expressions. We check this in the next step.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is the same expression written in a different form, so nothing new is learned
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even for the same expression, a new form can show which formula you can use.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: (x²+2)(2x), the product of (x²+2) and (2x), is exactly the same expression as x⁴+4
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A difference of squares is not the product of the two expressions but the product of their sum and difference. Expand to check.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It looks like a difference of squares so it seems possible, but we do not settle it before expanding to check
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This attitude uses a plausible shape as a clue, but does not settle it before checking.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is a difference of squares, so we see it can be written as a product of a sum and a difference
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You recognized the A²−B² form and recalled the formula. What remains is to check that the two quadratic expressions are right.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Expanding (x²+2x+2)(x²−2x+2) gives x⁴+4. (The x³ terms and the x terms cancel each other.)
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the final judgment on Minho's conclusion?
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.after: A product form actually comes out, so Minho's conclusion is wrong. However, the observation 'there is no real root' is right, and it means there is no linear factor. Both are judgments that state the same fact at different levels of precision.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Minho's conclusion is right. The two quadratic expressions cannot be split any further, so x⁴+4 cannot be factored
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It can already be written as a product, so x⁴+4 has been factored. Whether the two quadratic expressions can be split further is a separate matter.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The value was 4 or more, so this expansion result must be wrong
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The test of plugging in values only shows there is no linear factor. The expansion result can be checked by direct calculation.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The observation that there is no real root is right, but the part that drew 'cannot be factored' from it is wrong
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a precise judgment that accepts the observation and fixes only the leap.
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Minho's conclusion is wrong. x⁴+4 can be written as a product of two quadratic expressions
y-m-32-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You overturned the conclusion by giving a counterexample (the actual product form).
y-m-32-03.s.s1.reflect: If you chose 'premature' in step 1, how was that judgment confirmed in step 3? Say what factor the fact 'there is no value that makes it 0' shows is missing and what possibility it leaves open.
y-m-32-03.s.s2.prompt: Imagine explaining to Minho, and write separately the part of his observation that is right and the part of his conclusion that needs fixing.
y-m-32-03.s.s2.hint.0: Split the two sentences Minho said (the observation and the conclusion) apart.
y-m-32-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write one line of an expression you could use to rebut the conclusion.
y-m-32-03.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Your observation is right. ... But ...
y-m-32-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you separate the part of the observation that is right from the leap?
y-m-32-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you show with an expression the reason it can be factored?
y-m-32-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you state the difference between 'there is no linear factor' and 'cannot be factored'?
y-m-32-03.s.s2.model.0: Your observation is right. No matter what real number you plug in for x, x⁴+4 is 4 or more, so it is never 0, and so there is no linear factor of the form x−k. But the conclusion needs fixing. Even without a linear factor, it can be written as a product of two quadratic expressions, so it can be factored as (x²+2x+2)(x²−2x+2).
y-m-32-03.s.s2.model.1: It is true that there is no real root. That only means there is no linear factor. If you write x⁴+4=(x²+2)²−(2x)², it is a difference of squares and becomes a product of two quadratic expressions, so the part that says 'cannot be factored' needs fixing.

y-m-32-04.title: Can the expansion be wrong even though the check came out right?
y-m-32-04.topic: Multiplication formulas: the square of a sum of three terms and the limits of checking
y-m-32-04.goal: Find the wrong line in an expansion solution, confirm with a counterexample why a check using numbers failed to catch the error, and then choose a more trustworthy way of checking.
y-m-32-04.material: This is Hayun's record of expanding (x+2y−1)² and checking by plugging in numbers. (x and y are real numbers; y² means 'y squared' and 2y means '2 times y'.) Using the formula (A+B+C)²=A²+B²+C²+2AB+2BC+2CA, set A=x, B=2y, and C=−1.
y-m-32-04.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in the solution
y-m-32-04.thinking.1: Making a counterexample to an error that the check cannot catch
y-m-32-04.thinking.2: Evaluating the strategy of choosing values for checking
y-m-32-04.prereq.0: Able to read the expansion of (A+B+C)² (multiplication formula) (introductory level of the multiplication formulas in the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-04.prereq.1: Finding the value of an expression by plugging numbers in for letters
y-m-32-04.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-04.s.s1.prompt: In Hayun's record, choose the first line where the calculation is wrong.
y-m-32-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put the original values of B, C, and A into 2BC and 2CA and recalculate each.
y-m-32-04.s.s1.hint.1: For each line, tell apart whether it just copies the result of the previous line or was newly calculated.
y-m-32-04.s.s1.line.5: Check: with x=1, y=1, the left side is (1+2−1)²=4 and the right side is 1+4+1+4−2−4=4. They are equal, so it is right.
y-m-32-04.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. 2BC=2·2y·(−1)=−4y and 2CA=2·(−1)·x=−2x. The coefficients −2 and −4 were swapped. Line 5 carries over this result, and the check in line 6 is correct as a calculation but cannot notice this error.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.prompt: Hayun's final expression x²+4y²+1+4xy−2y−4x must differ in value from the original expression (x+2y−1)² for the error to show. Find 3 pairs (x, y) for which the values of the two expressions are different.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.hint.0: Try a case where you plug the same number into x and y and a case where you plug different numbers, putting each into both expressions and comparing.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.hint.1: In an example where the two values came out different, look at which term makes them differ.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please choose x and y so that their absolute values are 20 or less.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of the two expressions differ, so Hayun's error shows.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The values of the two expressions are the same, so the error does not show. Try other values.
y-m-32-04.s.s2.explain: The difference between the original expression and Hayun's expression is 2x−2y. If x=y, the difference is 0 and the values are equal, so the error is not caught. For a value with x≠y, for example (0, 1), the original expression gives 1 and Hayun's expression gives 3.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.prompt: What is the most appropriate reason Hayun's check (x=1, y=1) did not catch the error, and the best way to check in the future?
y-m-32-04.s.s3.hint.0: At the x=1, y=1 that Hayun used, find the values of −2y−4x and −4y−2x and compare them.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.hint.1: When x and y are not the same value, compare once more whether the two values are equal.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.o.a: The calculated value in the check was wrong, and using a calculator would fix this kind of error
y-m-32-04.s.s3.r.a: The check calculation itself was right. Look at whether the choice of values was the problem.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.o.b: Because x=y, the values of the two wrong terms became equal. We also plug in other values
y-m-32-04.s.s3.r.b: This thinking knows that one match is not a proof and tries to strengthen the check by choosing values differently.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.o.c: Checking by plugging in numbers is a method that cannot be used to check whether an expansion result is right
y-m-32-04.s.s3.r.c: Plugging in numbers can catch errors. Which values you plug in is what matters.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.o.d: One check is enough, so this was just a coincidence unrelated to the calculation
y-m-32-04.s.s3.r.d: One match is not a proof that the expansion is right. It can match even when there is an error.
y-m-32-04.s.s3.explain: If x=y, the wrong term −2y−4x and the right term −4y−2x become the same value. If you choose check values where x and y are different numbers, this error shows. One match is not a proof; it only means 'no mistake was found'.

y-m-32-05.title: If you know one value, is the remainder determined?
y-m-32-05.topic: Remainder when divided by a linear expression and by a quadratic expression: whether the information is sufficient
y-m-32-05.goal: Judge whether the given information determines the remainder, sort out what extra information is needed when it does not, and make a counterexample to information that sounds plausible but is insufficient.
y-m-32-05.material: You want to find the remainder when the polynomial f(x) is divided by (x−1)(x−2). All you know now is the single fact f(1)=3. The remainder has degree 1 or lower, so you can write it as ax+b (a and b are real numbers). That is, f(x)=(x−1)(x−2)·Q(x)+ax+b. (Q(x) is the quotient.)
y-m-32-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient or insufficient
y-m-32-05.thinking.1: Showing with several examples that it is not determined
y-m-32-05.thinking.2: Explaining with a counterexample why plausible extra information is insufficient
y-m-32-05.prereq.0: The remainder when a polynomial f(x) is divided by x−k is f(k), and you can use the division equation f(x)=(divisor)×(quotient)+(remainder) (introductory level of the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-05.prereq.1: The remainder when dividing by a quadratic expression can be written as ax+b, an expression of degree 1 or lower
y-m-32-05.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-05.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different remainders ax+b that do not contradict the information f(1)=3.
y-m-32-05.s.s1.hint.0: First check which term disappears when you plug x=1 into the division equation.
y-m-32-05.s.s1.hint.1: First choose a, then adjust b.
y-m-32-05.s.s1.ok.c1: The value when x=1 is plugged in is 3. It does not contradict f(1)=3.
y-m-32-05.s.s1.fail.c1: Plugging in x=1 means a+b must be 3. Right now it is not 3.
y-m-32-05.s.s1.explain: Plugging in x=1 makes (x−1)(x−2)Q(x) equal 0, so f(1)=a+b. So every (a, b) with a+b=3 is possible. The remainder can be 3, x+2, 3x, −2x+5, ..., many things, so f(1) alone does not determine the remainder.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.prompt: To determine the remainder as one, what would be enough to know in addition to f(1)=3? Choose all that are enough.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.hint.0: Change the value you plug in for x in the division equation and find which value makes the term multiplied by the quotient disappear.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write what expression in a and b the value of f becomes at that value, and count whether you get 2 equations.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.o.a: The value of f(0), that is, the value when x=0 is plugged in
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.a: Plugging in x=0 leaves the term multiplied by the quotient Q(0). Look at whether you can know the value of that term.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.o.b: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x−2
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.b: Look at whether this information tells you the value of the remainder ax+b when x=2 is plugged in.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.c: Think about whether a and b of the remainder are determined even if you know the degree.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.o.d: There is nothing more to know; it is already sufficient
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.d: The different remainders made in the earlier step all did not contradict f(1)=3.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.e: Look at whether plugging in x=2 makes the term multiplied by the quotient disappear.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.o.f: What degree the quotient Q(x) has
y-m-32-05.s.s2.r.f: Think about whether the value of the remainder is determined even if you know the degree of the quotient.
y-m-32-05.s.s2.explain: Plugging in x=2 makes (x−1)(x−2)Q(x) equal 0, so f(2)=2a+b. Combined with f(1)=a+b, a and b are determined as one. f(2) is the same information as 'the remainder when divided by x−2'. f(0) has the value of the quotient Q(0) mixed in, so it cannot tell you b directly.
y-m-32-05.s.s3.prompt: There are two polynomials, f₁(x)=x²−2x+4 and f₂(x)=2x²−3x+4, that both satisfy f(0)=4 and f(1)=3 (each gives 4 at x=0 and 3 at x=1). Find the remainder when each is divided by (x−1)(x−2), compare them, and write why the remainder is not determined even if you know f(0).
y-m-32-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the division equations for dividing f₁ and f₂ each by x²−3x+2 (the quotient equals the coefficient of x²).
y-m-32-05.s.s3.hint.1: Plug x=0 into both division equations and compare how much the term multiplied by the quotient is.
y-m-32-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The remainder of f₁ is ..., and the remainder of f₂ is ..., so ...
y-m-32-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check the calculation of writing f₁ and f₂ with (x−1)(x−2) as divisor, quotient, and remainder?
y-m-32-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect the reason f(0) is not directly equal to b of the remainder to the quotient?
y-m-32-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you conclude 'not determined' from the fact that the remainders are different?
y-m-32-05.s.s3.model.0: The remainder of f₁ is x+2 and the remainder of f₂ is 3x, so they are different. Both have f(0)=4 and f(1)=3, yet the remainders differ, so f(0) alone cannot determine it. f(0) has the value of the quotient at x=0 mixed in, so it is not directly equal to b of the remainder.
y-m-32-05.s.s3.model.1: f₁=(x−1)(x−2)·1+(x+2) and f₂=(x−1)(x−2)·2+3x. The quotients differ, 1 and 2, and plugging in x=0 makes the terms multiplied by the quotient 2 and 4, while b of the remainder is 2 and 0. Adding them, both give 4, so f(0) is the same. So even if you know f(0), the remainder is not determined as one.

y-m-32-06.title: Comparing four ways of finding the remainder
y-m-32-06.topic: Comparing and checking several ways of finding a remainder
y-m-32-06.goal: Compare several methods for the same remainder problem, sort out the valid methods from those with a leap, judge which is more convenient when the method changes, and check the result.
y-m-32-06.material: Find the remainder when f(x)=x²⁰−3x+2 (x to the 20th power minus 3x plus 2) is divided by x²−1. f(x)=(x²−1)·Q(x)+R(x), and Q(x) is a polynomial with integer coefficients. Five students used different methods. Method A: Write R(x)=ax+b, plug in x=1 and x=−1 to get f(1)=a+b and f(−1)=−a+b, and find a and b. Method B: Treat x²=1, change x²⁰=(x²)¹⁰=1, and regard f as equal to −3x+3. Method C: Since f(1)=0 and f(−1)=6, take the average of the two values, 3, as the remainder. Method D: Carry out the degree-20 long division all the way. Method E: Since f(1)=0, it is divisible by x−1, so regard it as divisible by x²−1 too and take the remainder to be 0.
y-m-32-06.thinking.0: Comparing and evaluating several solution methods
y-m-32-06.thinking.1: Finding the leap in a plausible but wrong method
y-m-32-06.thinking.2: Judging the range where a method applies
y-m-32-06.prereq.0: That the remainder when dividing a polynomial by a quadratic expression can be written as ax+b, and the calculation of f(k) (introductory level of the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-06.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the methods that can find the remainder correctly. (Include methods that take a long time but reach the correct result.)
y-m-32-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each method, write in one line what fact (the division equation, substitution) it starts from.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.hint.1: Plug the values of f(1) and f(−1) used in methods C and E into the remainder ax+b and check whether it is right.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.o.a: Method C (take the average as the remainder)
y-m-32-06.s.s1.r.a: f(1)=0 and f(−1)=6 are right, but think about whether there is a reason the average of the two values becomes the remainder. See what happens when you plug x=1 and x=−1 into ax+b.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.r.b: This is the flow of writing the remainder as ax+b and plugging in the values that make the divisor 0 to find a and b.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.o.c: Method E (since it is divisible by x−1, take it to be 0)
y-m-32-06.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether being divisible by x−1 is the same as being divisible by x²−1. Also look at the value of f(−1).
y-m-32-06.s.s1.o.d: Method B (replace x² with 1 to reduce)
y-m-32-06.s.s1.r.d: This method uses the fact x²=1 at the values that make x²−1 equal 0.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.o.e: Method D (carry out the degree-20 long division all the way)
y-m-32-06.s.s1.r.e: If you carry it out all the way, the correct remainder comes out, but it takes a lot of time.
y-m-32-06.s.s1.explain: A and B use the property of the values (1, −1) that make the divisor 0, and get R(x)=−3x+3. D takes long but gives the correct result. C has no basis for saying the remainder is the average of f(1) and f(−1), and for E, f(−1)=6, so it is not divisible by x+1.
y-m-32-06.s.s2.prompt: If the divisor changes from x²−1 to x²−3x+2=(x−1)(x−2), what happens to method A and method B? Write which one you would choose, with a reason.
y-m-32-06.s.s2.hint.0: First write how many values of x make the new divisor 0.
y-m-32-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write what you would replace x² with in method B, and follow what happens to x³.
y-m-32-06.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Method A is ..., method B is ... so ...
y-m-32-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why method A can be used in the same way with the new divisor?
y-m-32-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why method B becomes hard with the new divisor?
y-m-32-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is the reason for your choice connected to the range of the method (whether it can always be used)?
y-m-32-06.s.s2.model.0: Even if the divisor changes to (x−1)(x−2), A can be used the same way by plugging in x=1 and x=2 to get f(1)=a+b and f(2)=2a+b. B has to keep using x²=3x−2 to reduce the 20th power of x, so it is troublesome. So I choose A.
y-m-32-06.s.s2.model.1: B was fast thanks to the special property x²=1. If the divisor changes, it becomes x²=3x−2 and you have to keep replacing x³, x⁴, ..., which is complicated. In general, method A, which writes ax+b and uses f(1) and f(2), is safe. But when it is simple like x²−1, B is good too.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.prompt: You want to check after finding R(x)=−3x+3. What is a way to check something that must hold if R is right?
y-m-32-06.s.s3.hint.0: Move the remainder R(x) to one side of the division equation. Look at what the leftover expression is a multiple of.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.o.a: Plug in x=3 and check whether f(3) is a multiple of 8
y-m-32-06.s.s3.r.a: If the remainder is not 0, think about whether f(3) itself needs to be a multiple of 8.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.o.c: Check whether R(3) is a natural number less than 8
y-m-32-06.s.s3.r.c: The remainder is a condition on the degree of the expression, not a condition that its value is a natural number smaller than the divisor's value.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.explain: f(x)−R(x)=(x²−1)Q(x) and Q has integer coefficients, so at x=3, f(3)−R(3) is 8×(an integer). You can confirm that f(3)−R(3)=3486784400=8×435848050. f(3)=3486784394 leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 8, so it is not a multiple of 8, and a is not right.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.hint.1: Put a suitable integer in for x, find the value of x²−1, and check how it relates to f(x)−R(x).
y-m-32-06.s.s3.o.b: Put in x=3 and check whether f(3)−R(3) is a multiple of 8
y-m-32-06.s.s3.r.b: In the division equation, f−R is the product of x²−1 and the quotient. Connect it to the value of x²−1 at x=3.
y-m-32-06.s.s3.o.d: Put in x=3 and check whether f(3) and R(3) are the same value
y-m-32-06.s.s3.r.d: In f(x)=(x²−1)Q(x)+R(x), look at whether the term (x²−1)Q(3) is 0.

y-m-32-07.title: Is a cube the same when you add separately?
y-m-32-07.topic: The multiplication formula (a+b)³ and when it holds
y-m-32-07.goal: Work out for which cases the claim 'the cube of a sum of two numbers equals the sum of the cubes' holds, make examples where it holds yourself, and explain the condition with the expanded form.
y-m-32-07.material: Chaewon thinks (a+b)³=a³+b³. Her reason is that when she plugged in a=1 and b=0, the left side (1+0)³=1 and the right side 1³+0³=1 were equal. (a and b are real numbers. (a+b)³ means 'the cube of a plus b'.)
y-m-32-07.thinking.0: Telling apart weak tests and strong tests
y-m-32-07.thinking.1: Making examples where it holds yourself and discovering a rule
y-m-32-07.thinking.2: Explaining the condition for it to hold with the expanded form
y-m-32-07.prereq.0: Able to read (a+b)³=a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³ (introductory level of the multiplication formulas in the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-07.prereq.1: The fact that if a product is 0, one of its factors is 0
y-m-32-07.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-07.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Chaewon's evidence (equal at a=1, b=0)?
y-m-32-07.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine whether plugging a number other than 0 in for b would give the same result as a=1, b=0.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one pair where b is not 0 and calculate both sides.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.o.a: I found one pair that works, so it is fine to say it holds
y-m-32-07.s.s1.r.a: One pair holding does not guarantee 'all a and b'.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.o.b: One pair is not enough. We should test other pairs too
y-m-32-07.s.s1.r.b: This points out that the result of one pair cannot stand in for all cases.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.o.c: If b=0, the two sides are equal for any a, so this test is weak. We should test pairs where b is not 0
y-m-32-07.s.s1.r.c: This judgment even looks at how much information the test gives, that is, whether it is an easy test to pass.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.o.d: a=1 is a special value, so we only need to test when a is 2 or more
y-m-32-07.s.s1.r.d: The size of a does not decide the quality of a test. Think about which values you must plug in to tell the difference.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.explain: If b=0, the two sides are equal to a³ for any a, so the test is weak. But the point that one pair is not enough is also right.
y-m-32-07.s.s1.acc.0: It is a good judgment that b=0 is a weak test. It would be even better to also say that one pair is not enough.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different (a, b) with a≠0 and b≠0 for which (a+b)³=a³+b³ holds. (a=2, b=−2 and a=−2, b=2 count as the same example.)
y-m-32-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one nonzero number for a, then change b and calculate both sides.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.hint.1: Collect in a table what relationship a and b have in the pairs that work.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.ok.c1: Both a and b are not 0.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must not be 0.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The two sides are not equal. Calculate (a+b)³ and a³+b³ separately and compare.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.explain: (a+b)³−a³−b³=3ab(a+b). If a≠0 and b≠0, it is 0 only when a+b=0, so every pair with b=−a works. Examples: (1, −1), (2, −2), (5, −5).
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Write what the pairs you found have in common, and explain with the expanded form why only such pairs work.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the pairs that worked, 3 or more, on one line and calculate a+b.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The pairs I found are all ... Expanding (a+b)³ gives ...
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write exactly the relationship the pairs you found have in common?
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say why you write the difference of the two sides as a product?
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you say why the condition a≠0, b≠0 is needed?
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.model.0: The pairs I found all have a+b=0, that is, b=−a. Expanding (a+b)³ gives a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³, so (a+b)³−a³−b³=3ab(a+b). If a and b are not 0, it is 0 only when a+b=0.
y-m-32-07.s.s2.because.model.1: They were numbers with opposite signs and the same size (such as 2 and −2). The difference of the two sides can be simplified to 3ab(a+b), so if ab≠0 then a+b must be 0.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.prompt: If you remove the condition 'a≠0, b≠0', what pairs (a, b) satisfy (a+b)³=a³+b³?
y-m-32-07.s.s3.hint.0: Think about the cases where the difference of the two sides, 3ab(a+b), is 0, factor by factor.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.hint.1: Check which factor is 0 in a=1, b=0 and in a=1, b=−1.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.o.a: It holds only for pairs with b=−a, and not for any other pairs
y-m-32-07.s.s3.r.a: Think about the fact that Chaewon's first pair a=1, b=0 worked.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.o.b: It holds only for pairs with a=b, and not for other pairs
y-m-32-07.s.s3.r.b: Plug in a=b=1 and calculate both sides.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.o.c: Pairs where a=0 or b=0 or a+b=0
y-m-32-07.s.s3.r.c: This judgment gathers all the cases where the difference 3ab(a+b) is 0.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.o.d: It holds for all pairs, and no pair where it fails can be found
y-m-32-07.s.s3.r.d: You already found pairs where it does not hold earlier.
y-m-32-07.s.s3.explain: For (a+b)³−a³−b³=3ab(a+b)=0, one of a=0, b=0, a+b=0 must hold. Chaewon's first pair (1, 0) was the case b=0.

y-m-32-08.title: For which b can x²+bx+12 be split?
y-m-32-08.topic: Factoring quadratic expressions and the range (integers/reals)
y-m-32-08.goal: Systematically make quadratic expressions that factor into a product of linear expressions with integer coefficients, and tell apart that a case missing from the list may not be 'impossible' but 'depends on the range'.
y-m-32-08.material: In the quadratic expression x²+bx+12, b is an integer. You want to find the b for which this expression factors in the form (x+m)(x+n). (x² means 'x squared'.) First consider only the case where m and n are integers.
y-m-32-08.thinking.0: Finding all solutions without missing any under a restriction
y-m-32-08.thinking.1: Telling apart conclusions that change depending on the range (integers/reals)
y-m-32-08.prereq.1: The sign of the discriminant b²−4ac of a quadratic equation and real roots (middle school grade 3 to high school Common Math level)
y-m-32-08.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-08.s.s1.prompt: Find integers m and n such that (x+m)(x+n)=x²+bx+12, and the resulting b, with 4 different values of b. (Pairs where only the positions of m and n are swapped give the same b, so count them as one.)
y-m-32-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the coefficients, term by term, of the expanded expression x²+(m+n)x+mn and x²+bx+12.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find the integer pairs whose product is 12, starting from the smallest numbers, and find their sums.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.ok.c1: m, n, and b are integers.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.fail.c1: m, n, and b must be integers.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.ok.c2: The product of m and n is 12.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.fail.c2: The product of m and n is not 12. Compare with the constant term 12.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.ok.c3: The sum of m and n is b.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.fail.c3: The sum of m and n is not b. Compare with the coefficient of x.
y-m-32-08.s.s1.explain: Since (x+m)(x+n)=x²+(m+n)x+mn, we have mn=12 and b=m+n. The integer pairs with product 12 are (1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4), and the pairs that are all negative. So b can be six values: ±7, ±8, ±13.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.prompt: b=9 is not on the list. Yeonghui said, 'x²+9x+12 cannot be factored.' What do you think of this statement?
y-m-32-08.s.s2.hint.0: First look for an integer pair whose product is 12 and whose sum is 9.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the discriminant of x²+9x+12=0 and check its sign.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.o.a: x²+9x+12 factors as (x+3)(x+4), so Yeonghui's statement is wrong
y-m-32-08.s.s2.r.a: Check what the coefficient of x is when you expand (x+3)(x+4).
y-m-32-08.s.s2.o.b: It cannot be done with integers, but the discriminant is positive, so it can be done in the real numbers
y-m-32-08.s.s2.r.b: This points out that whether it can be factored depends on 'in what range of numbers' you ask the question.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.o.c: It cannot be factored in the integers or in the real numbers, so Yeonghui's statement is right
y-m-32-08.s.s2.r.c: Check the sign of the discriminant 81−48.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.o.d: Whether it can be factored is decided only by the constant term 12, regardless of b
y-m-32-08.s.s2.r.d: Even with the same constant term, the result changed when b changed.
y-m-32-08.s.s2.explain: The discriminant of x²+9x+12=0 is 81−48=33>0, so there are two real roots, and using those roots it can be written in the form (x−α)(x−β) in the real numbers. With integer coefficients, there is no integer pair whose product is 12 and whose sum is 9, so it cannot be done. So Yeonghui's statement is right only in the 'integer range'.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.prompt: If we allow products of linear expressions with not 'integer coefficients' but 'real coefficients', which integers b make x²+bx+12 factorable?
y-m-32-08.s.s3.hint.0: Find the sign of b²−48 for b=6 and for b=7.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.hint.1: On a number line, find the range of integers b that satisfy b²−48≥0.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.o.a: It is possible only for values found earlier such as b=±7, ±8, ±13, and not for other b
y-m-32-08.s.s3.r.a: Earlier we allowed only integers m and n. See what happens when the range of allowed numbers widens.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.o.b: We widened the range to the real numbers, so it can be factored for every integer b
y-m-32-08.s.s3.r.b: If b=6, the discriminant is 36−48. Check its sign.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.o.c: Integers b for which b²−48 is 0 or more, that is, b≥7 or b≤−7
y-m-32-08.s.s3.r.c: This expresses whether it can be factored as a condition by connecting it to the sign of the discriminant.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.o.d: It can be factored only when b is an even integer
y-m-32-08.s.s3.r.d: It also factored for an odd number such as b=7.
y-m-32-08.s.s3.explain: To factor in the real numbers, there must be real roots, so b²−48≥0. If b²≥48, then |b|≥7, so the integer b is 7 or more or −7 or less. For b from −6 to 6, it cannot be done even in the real numbers.

y-m-32-09.title: Even if an equation is true, can it fail to be the result of a division?
y-m-32-09.topic: Conditions for the quotient and remainder in polynomial division
y-m-32-09.goal: Show that the equation 'f=(divisor)×(quotient)+(remainder)' holding is not enough to call them the quotient and remainder, and understand why a condition on the degree of the remainder is needed for the answer to be determined as one.
y-m-32-09.material: This is a problem of dividing f(x)=x³+2x+1 by x−1. Jiho said 'quotient x²+x+3, remainder 4', and Sua said 'quotient x²+x+2, remainder x+3'. Both of them expanded and checked that f(x)=(x−1)×(quotient)+(remainder) holds. (x³ means 'x cubed'.)
y-m-32-09.thinking.0: Sorting out whether an equation is a necessary or a sufficient condition
y-m-32-09.thinking.1: Making examples that break the condition yourself
y-m-32-09.thinking.2: Explaining why the condition determines the solution as one
y-m-32-09.prereq.0: Multiplying and adding polynomials, and combining like terms
y-m-32-09.prereq.1: The convention that in the division equation A=BQ+R, the degree of R must be less than the degree of B (introductory level of the high school Common Math polynomial unit)
y-m-32-09.prereq.2: (Assumption) In this assignment, H1 only indicates difficulty and level of support; it does not mean that any course is taught in any particular grade. It is assumed to be an introductory level, after a student who learned multiplication formulas, factoring, and the basics of quadratic equations in middle school first encounters the polynomial unit of high school Common Math (polynomial operations, identities and remainder calculations, factoring).
y-m-32-09.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Sua's answer?
y-m-32-09.s.s1.hint.0: For each person, multiply the quotient by (x−1), add the remainder, and check whether the result equals f.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.o.a: The equation holds, so both are correct quotients and remainders, and there can be several quotients and remainders
y-m-32-09.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether checking that the equation is true is the same as checking that 'they are accepted as the quotient and remainder'.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.o.b: Jiho's answer, which has the larger quotient, is right
y-m-32-09.s.s1.r.b: The size of the quotient is not the criterion. The two people's quotients differ only in the constant term.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.o.d: We confirmed that the equation holds, but we also need to check the condition on the degree of the remainder
y-m-32-09.s.s1.r.d: This asks whether there is another condition needed to accept it as a result, without stopping at checking the equation.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.explain: The degree of the remainder must be less than the degree of the divisor. Sua's remainder x+3 has the same degree as the divisor x−1, so it breaks this condition. So Sua's equation is true but is not accepted as the 'result of a division'.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.prompt: Like Sua, write the quotient as x²+x+k and the remainder as px+q. Find 3 different (k, p, q) such that f(x)=(x−1)(x²+x+k)+px+q holds with p≠0. (k is an integer.)
y-m-32-09.s.s2.hint.0: Expand (x−1)(x²+x+k) and subtract it from f(x).
y-m-32-09.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one k and make a table of how the x coefficient and the constant term of the remainder change.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.var.p: p (coefficient of x in the remainder)
y-m-32-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The coefficient of x is right, so the equation holds.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The coefficient of x is not right. Expand (x−1)(x²+x+k) and compare the coefficient of x with f.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The constant term is right, so the equation holds.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.fail.c3: The constant term is not right. Compare the constant term of the expanded expression with f.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.ok.c4: This is an example where the remainder is linear, so it is not accepted as the result of a division.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.fail.c4: If p=0, the remainder is a constant, so it is the result of a division. This time, find examples with p≠0.
y-m-32-09.s.s2.explain: (x−1)(x²+x+k)=x³+(k−1)x−k, so subtracting this from f gives the remainder (3−k)x+(1+k). So p=3−k and q=1+k. If k=2, the remainder is x+3 (Sua's answer); if k=0, it is 3x+1; if k=1, it is 2x+2. Only when k=3 does p become 0, which is Jiho's answer.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.prompt: How many k make p=0, and because of that, what role does the condition 'the degree of the remainder is less than the divisor' play?
y-m-32-09.s.s3.hint.0: From p=3−k, find the k for which p is 0.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the examples with p≠0 you made in the earlier step satisfy the condition.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.o.a: There is only k=3, so adding this condition determines the quotient and remainder as one
y-m-32-09.s.s3.r.a: This judgment connects the number of k with p=0 to uniqueness.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.o.b: There are two, k=2 and k=3, so both are accepted even with this condition
y-m-32-09.s.s3.r.b: Recalculate the value of p when k=2.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.o.c: There is no such k, so there is no quotient that satisfies this condition
y-m-32-09.s.s3.r.c: Plug Jiho's answer into this form.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.o.d: There is only k=3, but answers with p≠0 have the same standing, so there are still several
y-m-32-09.s.s3.r.d: You checked in the earlier step what the criterion that sets the standing is.
y-m-32-09.s.s3.explain: If p=3−k=0, there is only k=3. So adding the condition 'the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor' determines the quotient x²+x+3 and remainder 4 as one. The equation alone does not determine it.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.hint.1: Put Jiho's and Sua's remainders side by side, compare each with the divisor x−1, and write down any noticeable difference.
y-m-32-09.s.s1.o.c: The remainder must be 0, so both Jiho's answer and Sua's answer are wrong
y-m-32-09.s.s1.r.c: The remainder is 0 only when it divides evenly. Find the value of f(1) and check whether it is divisible by x−1.
